subskill: boundaries and form: a supplement opened with a comma must be closed with a comma rather than a dash, and the main verb answers to the plural head rather than to the singulars inside the supplement
passage: Ice cores are read downward, and the deepest layers are also the ones most likely to have been thinned and folded by the weight of everything above them. The two deepest cores from this ice divide, a pair drilled within a hundred meters of each other in a single austral summer by one field party ______ the sequence of ash layers on which every later chronology has been built, and no one has yet funded a third hole to settle the matter.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The head of the subject is "The two deepest cores," a plural noun; "from this ice divide" and the appositive that follows it are modifiers, and the singulars "divide," "summer" and "field party" inside them are what make ", contradicts" sound right. The second requirement is that a supplement be closed with the mark that opened it: "a pair drilled within a hundred meters of each other in a single austral summer by one field party" begins after a comma, so it must end with a comma, which is why "— contradict" fails even though its verb is the right one.

subskill: boundaries and form: a colon may not stand between a verb and its object, and a subordinate clause needs a finite verb rather than a participle
passage: Conservators who sample old varnish work in milligrams. The analysis published last winter reported that the topmost layer of the altarpiece ______ larch resin, walnut oil, and a trace of lead white too fine to have been precipitated.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The clause introduced by "that" needs a finite verb, and "containing" supplies only a participle, leaving "the topmost layer of the altarpiece containing larch resin" with no predicate at all. The second requirement is punctuation: a colon cannot separate a verb from the object it governs, so "contained:" cuts the verb off from the list that completes it, and "containing:" is wrong on both counts.

subskill: boundaries and form: two independent clauses cannot be joined by a comma, and an event prior to a stated past moment takes the past perfect
passage: The observatory's logbook is the only record of that night, and it is written in a hand that even the staff of the time found difficult. When the plate was developed on the morning of the fourteenth, the smear near the limb was already familiar to everyone in the building ______ the same object three nights earlier, on a plate that was never printed, and had told nobody outside the dome.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: What stands on either side of the blank is a pair of independent clauses, and a comma cannot join them, so both options opening with a comma leave a splice. The second requirement is sequence: the photographing is earlier than the past moment at which the smear "was already familiar," and the clause that follows, "and had told nobody outside the dome," is itself in the past perfect, so "; the night assistant photographed" puts the earlier event in the same tense as the later one.

subskill: boundaries and form: a compound predicate takes no comma before the conjunction that joins its two verbs, and a possessive formed on a plural noun puts the apostrophe after the plural ending
passage: A whaling agent kept two sets of books, one for the owners and one for the crew, and the discrepancy between them was rarely accidental. Four coopers worked the season on this agent's payroll, and all four were paid out of the same accounts as the boat steerers. The agent entered every barrel twice ______ against the season's total, so that a share computed from either book alone came out wrong in a way nobody ashore could reconstruct.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: "entered every barrel twice and charged the coopers' wages against the season's total" is one subject governing two verbs, and a comma does not separate the halves of a compound predicate, which rules out both options that open with a comma. The second requirement is the apostrophe: the wages belong to the four coopers named in the sentence before, so the possessive is built on the plural, giving "coopers'" and not "cooper's."

subskill: boundaries and form: no mark separates a subject from its verb however long the subject grows, and the verb answers to the plural head rather than to the singulars inside the modifier
passage: Where a specimen was gathered matters as much as what it is, and a sheet whose locality is wrong is worse than no sheet at all. The sheets collected on the southern transect by a single student working from a badly copied gazetteer ______ two localities that no map of the district has ever carried, and neither can now be checked against a living population.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The head of the subject is "The sheets," a plural noun; "collected on the southern transect by a single student working from a badly copied gazetteer" is a modifier, and the singulars "transect," "student" and "gazetteer" inside it are what make "records" sound right. The second requirement is that nothing stand between a subject and its verb, however far apart the two have been pushed, so ", records" and ", record" are both punctuated wrongly.

subskill: form: a clause of requirement after 'demanded that' takes the base form of the verb, and the subject is a singular head standing in front of a modifier full of plurals
passage: The commissioners demanded that every copy of the returns made by the parish constables ______ to the clerk of the peace within a week of the assize, and they set a fine for each day a copy was late.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: "demanded that" introduces a clause of requirement, and such a clause takes the base form of the verb: "be delivered." The indicative forms are wrong for that reason alone. The second requirement is agreement, which disposes of "are delivered" and "were delivered" twice over: the head of the subject is "every copy," a singular expression, and the plurals "returns" and "constables" sit inside a modifier that cannot govern anything.

subskill: form: the second member of a "not ... but" pair must match the first in kind, and the verb answers to the singular head rather than to the plurals inside the modifier
passage: Wills that dispose of a working shop are litigated more often than wills that dispose of land, and this one has been litigated twice. The schedule attached to the will, drawn up by two appraisers who never once entered the composing room, does not list the matrices at all ______ the press, the frames and the standing type as a single lot, which is why nobody can now say how many founts the shop held.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The first member of the pair is the finite verb phrase "does not list the matrices at all," so the member introduced by "but" must be a finite verb phrase too, which is what "but recording" and "but to record" fail to supply. The second requirement is agreement: the head of the subject is "The schedule," a singular noun, and "two appraisers" belongs to the supplement, so "but record" answers to the appraisers rather than to the schedule.

subskill: form: the verb answers to a singular head across a long modifier, and the two members of a coordination must be of the same kind
passage: Radiocarbon dates from a single bog can disagree by centuries, and the usual explanation is that old carbon has been carried upward through the peat by roots. The one thing every reviewer of the shallowest meter of this bog has asked for ______ the samples from the northern edge of the cut and to publish the raw counts rather than the calibrated ranges.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The head of the subject is "The one thing," a singular noun, so "are to rerun" and "are rerunning" answer to "reviewer" or to the plurals in the modifier rather than to the subject. The second requirement is parallelism: the other member of the coordination is the infinitive "to publish the raw counts," so the first member must be an infinitive too, which is what "is rerunning" fails to supply.

subskill: form: the verb answers to a plural head across a modifier crowded with singulars, and a span running from a past point to the present takes the present perfect
passage: Move a tide gauge even a few hundred meters along a harbor wall and it begins a new record rather than continuing the old one, since a gauge records the sea only where it stands. That is the difficulty with this station, which was rebuilt twice in its first decade and then left alone. The rolls covering the first twelve years, a period in which the gauge was shifted twice and the datum recomputed by one clerk working alone, ______ in a crate beneath the stairs of the harbor office since the port authority was dissolved, and no copy of them exists anywhere else.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The head of the subject is "The rolls," a plural noun; "a period in which the gauge was shifted twice and the datum recomputed by one clerk working alone" is a supplement describing the twelve years, and the singulars inside it are what make "has been stored" and "was stored" sound right. The second requirement is aspect: the storing runs from the dissolution of the port authority to the present, and a span of that kind takes the present perfect, so "were stored" has the number right and the tense wrong.

subskill: boundaries and form: a supplement opened with a dash, and carrying commas of its own, is closed with the matching dash, and the main verb answers to the singular head in front of it
passage: Everything a seismograph yields depends on its clock, and a station whose timekeeping drifts produces arrival times that cannot be used at all. The drum record for the whole of that decade — kept, like the drums from the two stations upriver, in a shed that flooded twice ______ now the only evidence that the array was ever run continuously, and the flood damage has never been assessed.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The supplement "kept, like the drums from the two stations upriver, in a shed that flooded twice" is opened with a dash and already carries commas of its own, so the mark that closes it must be the matching dash rather than a third comma. The second requirement is agreement: the head of the subject is "The drum record," a singular noun, and "drums" and "stations" sit inside the supplement, so "are" has nothing in the subject to answer to.

subskill: boundaries and form: a dependent clause placed in front of its main clause is closed with a comma, and an event completed before a stated past moment takes the past perfect
passage: Recipe books kept by dyers record failures as much as successes, since a recipe that worked was rarely written down twice. The alum that season came from a new supplier, and the wool came from a flock nobody in the shop had handled before. The two together were enough to turn a whole dyeing, though the book blames only the water. By the time the guild inspector arrived to seal the bolts at the end of the week ______ the whole of the first batch, and the entry for those days names neither the supplier nor the flock.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: "By the time the guild inspector arrived to seal the bolts at the end of the week" is a dependent clause standing in front of its main clause, and a clause in that position is closed with a comma, so the two options that begin with "the dyer" run the two clauses together. The second requirement is sequence: the discarding was finished before the inspector arrived, and a "by the time" frame of that kind takes the past perfect, which is why ", the dyer discarded" is punctuated correctly and still wrong.

subskill: form: the verb answers to a singular head across a relative clause full of plurals, and a completed action fixed to a closed past interval takes the simple past rather than the present perfect
passage: Tanning is a slow trade, and a yard capacity is fixed less by its labor than by the number of pits it can keep in use at once. The yard on the river below the bark mill changed hands three times in the century after the fire, and each owner left the pits a little deeper than he found them. The row of pits cut into the bank, which the three families who worked the yard between the fire and the coming of the railway enlarged and relined more than once, ______ to its present depth in a single season, and the accounts for that year record no payment to any mason.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The head of the subject is "The row," a singular noun; "of pits cut into the bank" and the relative clause after it are modifiers, and the plurals "pits" and "families" inside them are what make "were recut" sound right. The second requirement is tense: the recutting is fixed to one finished season, and the accounts for that year are spoken of as closed, so a present perfect claims a link to the present that the passage does not make, which rules out "has been recut" despite its number.

subskill: boundaries and form: a colon rather than a comma introduces the element that a complete clause has promised, and the verb of that clause answers to a singular head across a long modifier
passage: Glass furnaces leave little behind, since the crucibles were broken up and the cullet resold. The one thing the excavators of the furnace on the heath were never able to settle ______ the crucibles were charged at all.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The head of the subject is "The one thing," a singular noun, and "the excavators of the furnace on the heath" belongs to the relative clause modifying it, so "remain: how" and "remain, how" answer to the excavators instead. The second requirement is the mark: the clause before the blank is grammatically complete and promises the thing that was never settled, and a colon is what delivers it, while a comma leaves "how the crucibles were charged at all" hanging off a finished clause.

subskill: boundaries and form: a supplement opened with a comma is closed with a comma rather than a dash, and the possessive is formed on the plural because the owners are several
passage: Before anyone consults a census return it has been copied at least twice, and each copying is a chance for a household to change size. Four districts lay along the river, and each was walked by its own enumerator. The printed abstract for those districts, the only figure any later historian has quoted ______ tallies by more than three hundred persons, and the registrar general put the difference down to fatigue.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The supplement "the only figure any later historian has quoted" is opened with a comma, so the mark that closes it is a comma and not a dash. The second requirement is the apostrophe: each of the four riverside districts was walked by its own enumerator, so the tallies belong to several people and the possessive is formed on the plural, giving "the enumerators'" rather than "the enumerator's."

subskill: form: the second member of a coordination must match the first in kind, and a plain infinitive rather than a perfect infinitive reports an action that follows the one before it
passage: Planning a polar depot means working backward from the day it must be reached, and an error of a week in the plan is an error of a hundred pounds of food. The committee that fitted out the second winter party resolved to lay the depot in the autumn ______ it in the following spring with whatever the ponies could still carry, and neither half of the plan was carried out as written.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The first member of the coordination is the infinitive "to lay the depot in the autumn," so the second must be an infinitive as well, which is what "and restocking" and "and having restocked" fail to supply. The second requirement is aspect: a perfect infinitive marks an action as already completed at the moment of the main verb, and the restocking was to follow the laying rather than precede it, so "and to have restocked" has the right kind and the wrong time.

subskill: form: an introductory participial phrase must modify the subject that follows it, and an action tied to a named past year takes the simple past rather than the present perfect
passage: Kilns are rebuilt more often than they are designed, and most of what a potter knows about drafts is learned by watching a stack fail. Having relined the firebox twice in a single winter and lost both firings to a wind that came down the valley after dark ______ the whole stack to the lee of the barn in the spring of that year, and no firing was lost there again.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The introductory phrase reports who relined the firebox and lost the firings, and that can only be the potter, so a subject of "the stack" leaves the participial phrase describing something that did no relining. The second requirement is tense: the move is tied to "the spring of that year," a named past moment, and the present perfect cannot attach to one, so "the potter has moved" gets the subject right and the tense wrong.

subskill: boundaries and form: a semicolon rather than a comma joins two independent clauses, and what follows a semicolon must itself be a clause with a finite verb
passage: A lighthouse log is kept to a form, and the keeper who departs from the form is usually the one with something to record. The keeper at the western light entered the weather at eight and at noon every day for eleven years ______ the state of the lamp only when it had failed, which is why the log reads as though the lamp failed more often than it did.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The material on either side of the blank is a pair of independent clauses, and a comma cannot join them, so ", he recorded" leaves a splice. The second requirement is that a semicolon stand between two clauses and not between a clause and a fragment: "he recording the state of the lamp" has no finite verb, so "; he recording" puts the right mark in front of the wrong thing and ", he recording" is wrong on both counts.

subskill: form: the sentence needs a finite main verb rather than a participle, and that verb answers to the plural head rather than to the singulars inside the supplement
passage: Every canal survey is a chain of borrowed levels, and an error in one bench mark travels the whole length of the line. The levels taken along the northern reach in the second summer, none of which the resident engineer checked against the tidal datum at the mouth, ______ the line by something under a foot over eleven miles, an error small enough to be argued about for thirty years.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The sentence has no other predicate, so the blank must hold a finite verb; "raising" and "having raised" leave the whole of it as one long noun phrase followed by a participle. The second requirement is agreement: the head of the subject is "The levels," a plural noun, and "none," "the resident engineer," "the tidal datum" and "the mouth" all sit inside the supplement, so "raises" answers to a singular that is not the subject.

subskill: form: a clause of requirement after 'ordered that' takes the base form of the verb, which is not the same as the plural indicative, and the clause still needs a finite verb rather than a participle
passage: Statutes written to be read aloud keep their sentences short and their penalties exact, and this hall governed itself by one. The wardens who governed the hall in the years after the plague ordered that the fine for taking an apprentice in a closed year ______ on the master rather than on the boy, and the two cases that survive from the decade were decided that way.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: "ordered that" introduces a clause of requirement, which takes the base form "fall"; the base form is identical to the plural indicative here, which is what makes "falls" look like the agreeing option, since the subject "the fine" is singular. The second requirement is that the clause have a finite verb at all, so "falling" cannot stand, and "fell" reports the fine as a past fact rather than as the thing ordered.

subskill: boundaries and form: a supplement opened with a dash and containing commas is closed with the matching dash, and an action fixed to a named past winter takes the simple past rather than the present perfect
passage: Wrecks are dated by their timbers, and timbers are dated by rings that may have been cut a generation before the ship was built. The oaks that gave the keelson and the two lowest strakes — a stand on the far side of the estuary, cleared for pasture within the decade ______ down in a single winter, and nothing in the parish accounts records who bought the timber or what was paid for it.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The supplement "a stand on the far side of the estuary, cleared for pasture within the decade" is opened with a dash and carries a comma inside it, so it is closed with the matching dash; a comma there would read as one more item in the supplement's own list. The second requirement is tense: the felling happened in one named winter and the parish accounts are spoken of as a closed record, so "— have been cut" claims a continuing relevance the passage does not support.

subskill: boundaries and form: no comma stands before the conjunction joining the two verbs of a compound predicate, and the verb answers to the singular head across a relative clause about two people
passage: An assay office is trusted because it is dull: the same marks, struck in the same order, year after year. The register kept by the two assayers who served the office between the rebuilding and the fire lists every parcel received ______ the weight after cupellation in a second column, so that a fraud in the first column can be caught by arithmetic alone.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: "lists every parcel received and records the weight after cupellation in a second column" is one subject governing two verbs, and no comma stands before the conjunction in a compound predicate, which disposes of both options opening with a comma. The second requirement is agreement: the head of the subject is "The register," a singular noun, and "the two assayers" belongs to the modifier, so "and record" answers to the assayers rather than to the register.

subskill: boundaries and form: a colon may not separate a verb from the list it governs, and the verb answers to the plural head rather than to the singulars inside the modifier
passage: Nobody burning lime can see inside the kiln. The ledgers kept at the draw hole by the burner on each shift ______ the hour of every charge, the weight of stone and coal, and the name of whoever drew the kiln, but they never once note the weather.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The head of the subject is "The ledgers," a plural noun, and the later pronoun "they" confirms it; "kept at the draw hole by the burner on each shift" is a modifier, so "gives" answers to the burner or the shift instead. The second requirement is punctuation: a colon cannot stand between a verb and the objects it governs, so "give:" cuts "give" off from the three things the ledgers record, and "gives:" is wrong twice.

subskill: form: an event completed before a stated past moment takes the past perfect, and the clause needs a finite verb rather than a participle
passage: What survives on a cave floor is less a stack of layers than a record of what has been dug out of it, and the earliest excavators here drove a trench down the middle and threw the spoil outside. Nothing they removed was sieved, and their notebooks give depths only to the nearest foot. When the modern team opened the north wall in the second season, they found that at some point before the earliest trench was cut the water table ______ the base of the deposit, and that everything below the fourth layer had been waterlogged for most of the Holocene.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The clause introduced by "that" needs a finite verb, so "having reached" and "reaching" leave the water table with nothing to do. The second requirement is sequence: the rise of the water table is placed "at some point before the earliest trench was cut," which is itself a past event inside a past narrative, and the parallel clause that follows uses "had been waterlogged," so "reached" flattens two moments that the sentence keeps apart.

subskill: boundaries and form: a supplement opened with a comma is closed with a comma rather than a dash, and a change measured across a closed interval of past years takes the simple past
passage: Salt pans are worked until the brine will no longer pay for the fuel, and the date at which it stopped paying is rarely the date anyone wrote down. The yield of the eastern pans, which the ledgers report to the nearest bushel for every year between 1688 and the closure ______ by about a third across those four decades, and the fall is steady enough that no single cause will account for it.
prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: The supplement "which the ledgers report to the nearest bushel for every year between 1688 and the closure" is opened with a comma, so the mark closing it is a comma rather than a dash. The second requirement is tense: the fall is measured across an interval that begins in 1688 and ends at the closure, a stretch of time shut at both ends, and the present perfect cannot report a change confined to a finished period, which is why ", has fallen" is punctuated correctly and still wrong.
